newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs seek united NATO front before Madrid summit.
newsitem.headline: Czechs seek united NATO front before Madrid summit.

text.p: President Vaclav Havel gathered leaders of the four largest Czech political parties on Thursday in an attempt to convince somewhat reluctant Czech citizens that joining NATO is a good thing.

With opinion polls showing about half the country is still not convinced, and with the largest opposition party calling for a referendum on the issue, Havel emerged from a two-hour meeting to say that the leaders were sure that the country should be in NATO.

"In front of the domestic and foreign public I can, after today's meeting, clearly announce that all participants consider accession to the North Atlantic treaty and... future membership in the North Atlantic alliance as a great, historic chance for our country," Havel said, reading from a prepared text.

Polls show that compared with citizens in Poland and Hungary, the other two nations also widely expected to be invited to join NATO at a summit of the alliance in Madrid in less than two weeks, the Czechs are cool on the idea.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and key members of the three centre-right ruling coaltion parties joined leaders of the largest party in the Czech Republic's opposition, the Social Democrats, to stand behind Havel as he read the statement.
Havel has made NATO membership his primary foreign policy goal since helping lead the non-violent "Velvet Revolution" that toppled Communist rule in 1989.

He said on Thursday that the parties in the group, which took 80 percent of the votes in 1996 parliamentary elections, felt NATO membership was the first chance for democratic Prague to take part in the "collective defence of values".

"Membership in NATO, as the participants in today's meeting agreed, doesn't mean for us only international guarantees of our security, but also obligations of joint responsibility for others' security," Havel said.
His statement added that "the Czech Republic is fully prepared" to accept all obligations of membership.

Western politicians, such as Senator Joseph Biden who is the most senior backer of NATO expansion in the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, have said that Czech officials need to do more to foster public support for membership.
Biden said in April that approval of NATO expansion in the Senate was "not a done deal" and it would help if the Czech public showed that they really wanted to join.
The joint Czech political declaration on Thursday said the participants had agreed to explain to the public in coming months the importance of NATO membership including its costs and benefits.
None of the leaders would take questions from journalists after the declaration.

Still unanswered was whether the Social Democrats, currently the most popular party according to the polls, had dropped their demand for a referendum on NATO membership. Officially, the party supports joining the U.S.-led alliance.
Social Democrat chairman Milos Zeman, who took part in the meeting, was not immediately available for comment.
